Collaboration, communication, and teamwork are all linked to stronger safety outcomes in the literature. Organizations whose various teams collaborate and communicate openly and effectively tend to enjoy superior patient safety outcomes.    

### Why is it important?

In today's healthcare environment of specialization and more clinicians being involved in the care process, patients are more likely to interact with more individuals and care teams than in the past. For example, for a typical 4-day hospital stay, a patient is likely to interact with up to 50 different employees including physicians, nurses, technicians, transport, and administrative personnel. As patients are "handed-off" to these different individuals and departments, the likelihood of miscommunication and ultimately safety errors goes up. Solid communication and teamwork across these different groups is essential for quality care. **Below are some suggested actions to improve collaboration.**

- **Use structured communication techniques**  
In their chapter in the Patient Safety and Quality Handbook, O'Daniel and Rosenstein concluded that when a team needs to share complex information quickly, it is useful to use these to ensure accuracy.  Examples of structured communication techniques that might work for your organization include Crew Resource Management (CRM), SBAR (Situation-Background-Assessment-Recommendation), Read Back/Call Back, I-PASS (Illness severity, Patient Summary, Action list, Situation awareness & contingency plans, Synthesis by receiver)  and STICC (Situation Task Intent Concern Calibrate).

- **Manage risk through time-out's**  
When an employee on the care team senses a risk in care delivery, allow them to use a word or phrase that stops the situation so everyone can pause and carefully reassess the situation.  According to the Institute for Healthcare Improvement, these "time-outs" can help improve safety and are a hallmark of strong teams.

- **Conduct an organizational assessment to understand your level of collaboration**  
According to O'Daniel and Rosenstein, assessment information can be gained from formal methods such as incident reports, survey tools, focus groups, department meetings, task forces or committees, direct observation, suggestion boxes, and hot lines. Informal methods such as casual meetings and gossip can also provide valuable surface information and should be evaluated more deeply as to the source, relevance, and significance of the events to determine next steps. When you have a better sense of how your various teams collaborate, you can begin to address these issues.  

- **Create opportunities for connection across teams**  
Allowing time for employees to interact with one another and build relationships can also be valuable for stronger collaboration and teamwork. These activities can be formal or informal according to O'Daniel and Rosenstein. Examples include interdisciplinary committees, pre-op and post-op briefings, and organized meals with different team members.

- **Set up a standard set of guidelines for professional communication and behavior**  
Disruptive behavior and/or abuse of hierarchical position severely undermine teams ability to collaborate and communicate with one another. For example, individuals may be afraid to speak up because they are afraid of getting into a verbal altercation with a verbally abusive co-worker.  These standards must be set and all individuals - regardless of position or status - must be held accountable to these standards.  

>Sources:

>Frankel A, Haraden C, Federico F, Lenoci-Edwards J. A Framework for Safe, Reliable, and Effective Care. White Paper. Cambridge, MA: Institute for Healthcare Improvement and Safe & Reliable Healthcare; 2017. (Available on ihi.org)
